idiom_name: non-virtual public functions + private virtual *_impl hooks (Sutter's Virtuality guidelines)
implementation_notes: The C++ home of the idiom: members are non-virtual by default, so the wrapper needs no keyword and each customisation point is a private virtual, made protected only when derived classes must call the base implementation. Sutter's four guidelines are the checklist - prefer non-virtual interfaces (Template Method), prefer private virtuals, protected only for base calls, and give the base class a public virtual or protected non-virtual destructor. Clients still see polymorphic behaviour through the base class; derived classes cannot restate the interface. `override` on hooks (C++11) turns a signature drift into a compile error.
pitfalls: A derived overload with the same name hides the base wrapper instead of overriding it; call through a base reference and keep hook names distinct (read_impl).
Never call the hook from a constructor or destructor - during construction and destruction virtual dispatch stops at the class being built or torn down.
The destructor is the documented exception to the non-virtual rule: make it public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual.

variants.name: Handle/body (Pimpl) NVI: a fully non-virtual public class over an implementation hierarchy
variants.idiom_name: non-polymorphic handle class dispatching to a polymorphic implementation (Pimpl/Bridge)
variants.implementation_notes: The stronger separation Sutter points to: the public class has no virtual members and no virtual destructor at all - it holds a pointer to an implementation hierarchy and forwards, so every virtual call is behind a non-virtual facade. The handle is ABI-stable, implementation swaps (including test doubles) are invisible to clients, and the header no longer leaks the hierarchy. Combine with Bridge when the abstraction must vary independently of the implementation. It costs a heap allocation, one more indirection and an explicit copy policy (non-copyable, deep copy or copy-on-write).
pitfalls: Forgetting the copy policy: the compiler-generated copy would share one implementation object (typically leading to double-free); delete, deep-copy or reference-count explicitly.
Do not expose the implementation type in the public header - if clients can name it, they can override it and the ABI-stability and non-virtual guarantees both disappear.
Every call now pays one heap indirection; keep the handle small and avoid Pimpl for value-like or very hot types.
